clue.text: College has exotic trees planted by crank

indicators.note: planted by means set down beside, so the rearranged trees come next to the crank

parts.note: to crank is to wind with a handle, as one does a winch

indicators.note: exotic trees are strange and foreign, so the letters of trees are made unfamiliar by rearranging

explanation.surface: A college boasts unusual imported trees put in the ground next to a starting handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exotic' is the anagram signal and 'planted by' places its result beside the crank. The college is the famous English public school in Hampshire, founded in the fourteenth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Winchester College is one of England's oldest public schools, in the Hampshire cathedral city.

clue.text: Refuse, you say, to specify this body-part

indicators.note: you say signals that the word for refuse is to be taken by how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: refuse as a noun is rubbish or waste

explanation.surface: A person declines to name the part of the body in question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb, but it is the noun for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: The waist is the narrow part of the trunk between the ribs and hips.

clue.text: Remains of bread and butter?

parts.note: sounds like leftover crumbs, but bread and butter is one's living and the remains are earnings after deductions

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is left of a sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread and butter' is the idiom for a basic livelihood; what remains of it after tax is take-home pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Net income is earnings left after tax and deductions.

clue.text: The sailors' duet when adrift in calm waters

indicators.note: adrift means loose and wandering off course, so the letters of the phrase float into a new order

explanation.surface: Two seamen sing together while their boat floats becalmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when adrift' turns the letters of THE SAILORS DUET into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: These subtropical belts of light winds and calms around thirty degrees north and south becalmed sailing ships.

clue.text: Upsetting reports about son in part of school year

indicators.note: about means going around the letter for son
upsetting in a down clue means turning the word over, so it is read from the bottom up

parts.note: reports are loud noises, like gunshots

explanation.surface: Distressing school reports mention a boy in the middle of term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' turns NOISES into SESION, and 'about' puts it around S. 'reports' looks like school reports but means bangs.
explanation.definitionFit: A session is a term of teaching, and in Scotland the whole academic year.

clue.text: Under a day before spider achieves the greatest height

indicators.note: under in a down clue sets the spider's letters beneath those of the day before

parts.note: eve is the day before a festival, as with Christmas Eve
in snooker a spider is a rest with raised legs that lifts the cue over a ball

explanation.surface: Just before a deadline, a spider makes its highest climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under' puts REST below EVE in this down clue. A spider is a raised cue rest in snooker.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Everest is the world's highest mountain, the summit of the planet.

clue.text: Article finally exposes character on the staff

indicators.note: exposes means lays bare a run of letters that sits across the two words Article and finally

explanation.surface: A newspaper article ends by unmasking some person on the payroll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exposes' shows the letters spanning the end of 'Article' and the start of 'finally'. The 'staff' is the musical stave, not a workforce.
explanation.definitionFit: A clef is the symbol at the start of a musical stave fixing the pitch of its lines.

clue.text: He's landed face-up right in it

indicators.note: in means the letter for right goes inside
up in a down clue means the word for face is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a dial is a face, as of a clock

explanation.surface: A man lands flat on his back, exactly in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DIAL into LAID, and 'in' puts R inside. 'landed' is not arriving but owning land; a laird is a Scottish landowner.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird is a Scottish owner of a landed estate.

clue.text: It offers a choice for those entering pools

definitions.text: It offers a choice for those entering pools

parts.words: It offers a choice for those entering pools
parts.note: reads like football pools betting, but it is a swimming race where any stroke may be chosen

explanation.surface: Something gives options to people filling in football pools coupons.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'pools' suggest Britain's football pools betting; they are swimming pools.
explanation.definitionFit: In freestyle swimming events the competitor may use any stroke, nearly always front crawl.

clue.text: Walkabout — how like our monarch!

definitions.meaning: a walk about for health, a stroll taken for exercise
the British sovereign reigns under a constitution with limited powers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Walkabout' suggests a royal meeting the crowds, but here is a health stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: A constitutional is a walk taken for health; Britain's sovereign is a constitutional monarch.

clue.text: American doctors operating using Buggins' method, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells the solver that the phrase before it is to be taken by its sound when spoken

parts.note: Buggins' turn is the British idiom for jobs handed out by rotation, so working that way is acting in turns

explanation.surface: American medics take it in rotation to perform surgery, by seniority rather than merit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' signals a sound-alike: IN TURNS. Buggins' turn is a British phrase for promotion by rotation rather than merit.
explanation.definitionFit: In US usage, interns are junior hospital physicians in their first year of training after medical school.

clue.text: Zola's initial reason for moving

parts.note: the French novelist Zola's first name was Emile, so his initial is E
a motive is a reason for doing something

explanation.surface: The novelist's first letter explains why a thing was shifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zola's initial' looks like the letter Z, but it is the initial of his first name, Emile.
explanation.definitionFit: Something emotive stirs the feelings, as anything touching or affecting does.

clue.text: Break down as offer is beginning to excite

parts.note: a tender is a formal offer, as in a bid for a contract

indicators.note: beginning to points at the opening letter of the word excite that follows

explanation.surface: Something collapses when an offer starts to arouse interest.
explanation.definitionFit: To tenderise meat is to soften it by breaking down its fibres, by beating or marinating.

clue.text: Teams second before 13th July, for instance

parts.note: in the Roman calendar the ides was the middle day of a month, the 13th in most months

explanation.surface: Sporting teams arrive a moment before a mid-July date.
explanation.walkthrough: The ides fell on the 13th in most months but on the 15th in July; 'for instance' covers the setter's looseness about the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Sides are the opposing teams in a game or contest.

clue.text: A sort of nose mostly okay for smell

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all of the word is kept, so its final letter goes

parts.note: a Roman nose is one with a prominent high bridge

explanation.surface: Someone with a hooked nose can smell reasonably well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last letter of ROMAN; 'okay for' is the link, saying the result will do for the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An aroma is a distinctive, usually pleasant scent.

clue.text: About to get gold medal in sporting event

indicators.note: about means the gold medal pair wraps around the word to

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
a cross is a medal, as with the Victoria Cross
to is taken as its own letters

explanation.surface: Someone is on the verge of winning gold at a sporting event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'About' is the container signal: 'gold medal' wraps round 'to'. Autocross is motor racing over rough grass courses.
explanation.definitionFit: Autocross is a motor sport of timed racing over a grass or dirt circuit.

clue.text: Morning gathering for children to sing

definitions.text: Morning gathering for children to sing

parts.words: Morning gathering for children to sing
parts.note: a playground rhyme children sing about going gathering on a cold and frosty morning

explanation.surface: Youngsters assemble early in the day for a singsong.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'gathering' looks like an assembly of people, but in the rhyme it is picking fruit from hedges in the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional song runs 'Here we go gathering nuts in May on a cold and frosty morning'.

clue.text: High speed isn't breaking hand that turns

parts.note: Mach one is the speed of sound, written MACH I

indicators.note: breaking means the letters of isn't are smashed into a new order

explanation.surface: A fast pace isn't damaging the hand that steers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' turns ISNT into NIST. 'hand' is a worker, here one who turns metal on a lathe.
explanation.definitionFit: A machinist operates machine tools, such as a lathe turning metal; a factory hand is a worker.

clue.text: Flower-girl replacing centre of third cape

indicators.note: replacing centre of means the middle letter of the word third is swapped out for the girl

parts.note: Eliza Doolittle sells flowers in Shaw's Pygmalion and in My Fair Lady

explanation.surface: A girl selling flowers takes the place of the middle child of three by the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacing centre of' swaps the middle I of THIRD for ELIZA. The Lizard is the headland in Cornwall forming mainland Britain's most southerly point.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lizard is a peninsula and point on the Cornish coast, a promontory that counts as a cape.

clue.text: Zola, for example, presenting a small volume to employer

parts.note: cc is cubic centimetres, a small measure of volume
an employer is one who employs or uses something, a user

explanation.surface: The novelist hands a slim book to his boss.
explanation.walkthrough: Zola's open letter 'J'accuse' accused the French authorities over the Dreyfus affair. 'volume' looks like a book but is a measure.
explanation.definitionFit: Emile Zola famously accused the French army of a cover-up in his letter J'accuse.

clue.text: Row past sandy ridge in faraway port

indicators.note: past means coming after, so the row's letters follow the sandy ridge

parts.note: a dune is a ridge of sand
a din is a row, a loud noise

explanation.surface: Someone rows past a sandbank to reach a distant harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like rowing a boat but is a noise. Dunedin is a port city in New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: Dunedin is a harbour city in New Zealand's South Island, about as far from Britain as one can go.

clue.text: He may take some interest if you pop in his shop

definitions.text: He may take some interest if you pop in his shop

parts.words: He may take some interest if you pop in his shop
parts.note: reads as a friendly shopkeeper, but pop is slang for pawning goods and interest is the charge on the loan

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper might pay attention if you drop by.
explanation.walkthrough: In old British slang a pawnbroker is called this relative, and to 'pop' something is to pawn it.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang names a pawnbroker after a family relation, as in 'my watch is at my uncle's'.

clue.text: Create right fuss after Company cancel steamer for island

indicators.note: after places the right and the trimmed fuss behind the company abbreviation
cancel means strike out, so the steamer's letters are removed from the fuss

parts.note: fuss is taken as its own letters before the cut
SS stands for steamship, a steamer

explanation.surface: A firm calls off a ferry sailing, causing a proper row about which island to visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cancel' strikes the steamer out of the fuss, and 'after' puts the rest behind the company. 'Create' is only a link word, and the island is Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Corfu is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea, off the coast of Albania.

clue.text: This magistrate always sent up without quarter

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the reversed word surrounds the quarter
sent up in a down clue means the word for always is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: ever means always
E for east is one of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: A judge is forever mocked and shown no mercy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent up' turns EVER into REVE, and 'without' (outside) puts it around E. 'without quarter' looks like 'without mercy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a medieval English local official with judicial duties, such as the shire reeve or sheriff.

clue.text: State of string in an instrument, maybe

definitions.meaning: a state is the ... something is in, its shape or health
a string attached is a stipulation, and a legal instrument such as a will or contract can contain one

explanation.surface: Someone reports on how worn the string is in a violin or guitar.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'string' and 'instrument' suggest music; really they are a stipulation and a legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: A condition is both a state of being and a stipulation laid down in an agreement.

clue.text: Well-known saw

definitions.meaning: saw as a past verb means observed or took note of

explanation.walkthrough: 'saw' looks like the tool or a proverb, but it is the past of see.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means both famous and, as a verb, observed.

clue.text: Integration achieved by single head

parts.note: single means one
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: Unity is reached under one leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' looks like a leader but is the geographical headland, NESS, common in British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Oneness is unity, the state of being joined into a single whole.

clue.text: His pulling out may hasten loss of set

definitions.text: His pulling out may hasten loss of set

parts.words: His pulling out may hasten loss of set
parts.note: reads like someone withdrawing from a tennis set, but it is a practitioner extracting teeth one by one from the full set

explanation.surface: A player's withdrawal could speed up the loss of a tennis set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulling out' and 'set' suggest sport; the set is of teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A dental surgeon extracts teeth, and each extraction leaves the set of teeth smaller.

clue.text: Notice pipe's beginning to leak

parts.note: to notice is to see

indicators.note: beginning picks out the opening letter of the word pipe's

explanation.surface: Someone spots the moment a pipe starts to leak.
explanation.definitionFit: To seep is to ooze slowly out through small openings, as a liquid does through a crack.

clue.text: After dropping one, coach gets criticised and moved

indicators.note: dropping means letting fall, so the letter for one leaves the coach

parts.note: to coach is to train
I is the Roman numeral for one
slated means harshly criticised

explanation.surface: A coach who loses a player is panned by the press and transferred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' removes I from TRAIN to give TRAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Translated means moved from one place to another, used of a bishop changing see or relics being transferred.
